title: Genesis Apocryphon (1Q20) — Hobah Translation
about: The Genesis Apocryphon (1Q20, formerly 1QapGen) is an Aramaic retelling and expansion of stories from Genesis, especially traditions concerning Noah and Abraham. The surviving scroll is badly damaged: the opening columns are fragmentary and later columns are much more continuous. The work is not simply a copy of Genesis but an interpretive narrative in its own voice.

translation.status: Hobah provisional source-language reading translation of major preserved 1Q20 passages
translation.base_text: The Aramaic manuscript 1Q20 from Qumran Cave 1, following standard column sequence and publicly accessible manuscript readings
translation.method: Fresh modern-English rendering from the recoverable Aramaic sense. This edition translates coherent preserved narrative units and marks the severe gaps rather than inventing a continuous missing beginning.
translation.confidence: Medium-high in the continuous Abraham columns; medium or lower in the broken Noah material and uncertain restorations
translation.notes: The surviving text is presented as an apocryphal Genesis retelling, not as lost canonical verses. Brackets indicate broken or uncertain wording.
translation.license_note: The ancient Aramaic manuscript is public domain. Hobah English wording is newly prepared for this project.

chapters.label: Fragmentary opening — Lamech's fear
chapters.text: [Much of the beginning is lost.] Lamech looked upon the child who had been born and was troubled by his extraordinary appearance. He feared that the conception might have come from the Watchers or from the holy ones rather than from him. His heart was disturbed, and he spoke urgently to Bitenosh his wife, demanding that she tell him the truth about the child's conception.

chapters.label: Bitenosh's oath
chapters.text: Bitenosh answered Lamech with grief at his suspicion. She swore by the Great Holy One, by the King of the ages, that the seed was Lamech's and that the child had been conceived by him. ‘Remember my tenderness and the pleasure of our union,’ she said in substance. ‘This pregnancy is from you, not from a stranger, a Watcher, or a son of heaven.’ Lamech remained astonished and sought further assurance.

chapters.label: Enoch is consulted
chapters.text: Lamech went to Methuselah and told him what had happened. Methuselah travelled to Enoch, who was dwelling far away, and asked him about the child. Enoch explained that the birth was connected with events God had already made known concerning the coming judgment. The child truly belonged to Lamech, but his generation would witness extraordinary things.

chapters.label: Noah and the coming judgment
chapters.text: Enoch spoke of corruption upon the earth and of judgment coming upon violent flesh. The child would survive the destruction and become the beginning of a renewed generation. Methuselah was told to return and reassure Lamech. [The intervening columns are heavily damaged, and only portions of the Noah narrative can be followed.]

chapters.label: After the flood
chapters.text: In the more continuous Noah material, the earth is renewed after the waters. Noah offers worship, receives the land, and speaks about the ordering of his descendants. The narrative expands the Genesis story with first-person reflections, visions, and details about the inheritance of the earth. Portions dealing with planting and the vineyard survive among damaged lines.

chapters.label: Division of the earth
chapters.text: Noah describes portions of the earth and the inheritance assigned among his sons. Mountains, rivers, seas, and regions appear in the geographical account. The land is not divided randomly: its boundaries belong within a divinely ordered world. [Many place names and lines in this section are damaged or debated.]

chapters.label: Abram enters the story
chapters.text: The narrative turns to Abram and recasts his journey in first-person form. Abram leaves the land of the Chaldeans and travels according to the divine command. He describes the land through which he passes and the altars he builds. The retelling enlarges brief biblical notices into the reflections of the patriarch himself.

chapters.label: A dream before Egypt
chapters.text: Before entering Egypt Abram sees a troubling dream. A cedar and a date palm appear together; men come intending to cut down the cedar while leaving the palm. The palm cries out and prevents the cedar from being destroyed. Abram understands that the dream concerns himself and Sarai: his life will be endangered because of her beauty, but through her action he will be preserved.

chapters.label: Sarai's beauty
chapters.text: When the Egyptians see Sarai, they are astonished at her beauty. A description of her appearance is placed in the mouths of those who report her to Pharaoh: her face, eyes, hair, hands, and form are praised. The narrative makes explicit why the court desires her and why Abram fears for his life. Sarai is taken into the royal household while Abram is treated favourably because of her.

chapters.label: Pharaoh's affliction
chapters.text: After Sarai is taken, Pharaoh and his household are struck by an afflicting spirit and are unable to approach her as intended. For a period the plague remains upon the king and his house. Pharaoh's officials eventually learn that Sarai is Abram's wife and that the affliction is connected with the wrong done to them.

chapters.label: Abram prays for Pharaoh
chapters.text: Pharaoh summons Abram and asks him to pray so that the affliction may depart. Abram lays hands in prayer, and the evil spirit is rebuked and leaves the king. Pharaoh then recognizes the seriousness of what has happened. Sarai is restored to Abram, and gifts and possessions accompany their departure from Egypt.

chapters.label: Abram and Lot
chapters.text: Abram returns to the land with wealth, livestock, and servants. The growth of the households leads to conflict between the herdsmen of Abram and Lot. Abram chooses peace rather than rivalry and allows Lot to select his region. Lot looks toward the well-watered plain, while Abram remains in the land appointed to him.

chapters.label: The land shown to Abram
chapters.text: After Lot separates from him, Abram is shown the breadth of the land. He travels through its regions and views the inheritance promised to his descendants. The apocryphon expands the biblical command to look north, south, east, and west into a geographical journey of possession by sight.

chapters.label: The war of the kings
chapters.text: The later preserved narrative recounts the coalition of kings, the capture of Lot, and Abram's response. Abram gathers trained men and pursues the invaders. He defeats them and rescues Lot together with the captives and possessions. The story follows Genesis while adding narrative details and the patriarch's perspective.

chapters.label: Melchizedek and the recovered goods
chapters.text: On Abram's return, the king of Sodom comes to meet him, and Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of the Most High God, appears in the narrative. Abram refuses to enrich himself from the king of Sodom's property beyond what is justly due to those who accompanied him. [The scroll becomes fragmentary again beyond the preserved narrative.]
